content: In the Imperial and U.S. customary systems, a bushel is typically divided into eight local gallons. The abbreviation for a bushel is either bsh or bu. In the U.S. system, one bushel is equivalent to 35.23907017 liters, which is also equal to 8 corn or dry gallons, or 9.309177489 wine or liquid gallons. In the Imperial system, one bushel equals 36.36872 liters, which is equivalent to 8 Imperial gallons. When grains are bought and sold on commodity markets or at local grain elevators, or when grain production is reported, the bushel is treated as a unit of mass. For example: Oats: In the United States: 32 pounds (approximately 14.515 kilograms) In Canada: 34 pounds (approximately 15.422 kilograms) Barley: 48 pounds (approximately 21.772 kilograms) Malted Barley: 34 pounds (approximately 15.422 kilograms) Maize (corn): 56 pounds (approximately 25.401 kilograms) Wheat and soybeans: 60 pounds (approximately 27.215 kilograms) Other commodities, such as oilseeds, fruits, vegetables, coal, and even hair, have specific bushel weights defined, which can vary depending on the jurisdiction. In the United States, these definitions may differ from state to state. The U.S. government has been working to phase out traditional units like the bushel in favor of the metric system, which is used globally for scientific, technical, and most practical purposes. As a result, it is important to understand how the bushel relates to its metric equivalent and whether it is being used as a unit of mass or volume in a given context. The term bushel has also been used historically to translate foreign units of similar size and origin, such as the German Scheffel. During the Middle Ages, a bushel of wheat was defined as weighing 64 tower pounds. However, when the tower system was abolished in the 16th century, the bushel was redefined to weigh 56 avoirdupois pounds. During the Middle Ages, the bushel was rarely used in Scotland, Ireland, or Wales. Additionally, prior to the 19th century, there were even more variations of gallons in use, which further complicated the standardization of the bushel.
